Last week, from November 2 to 8, our engineering organization merged 1,119 pull requests into Perfloop, pushing the repository past 39,000 commits on main since April. That is the weekly throughput of a very large software company, except every engineer in the org is a coding agent running on Amp, and I run the whole company through a single chat thread.

What nobody tells you before you run a fleet of agents at that scale is that when you tell them to organize themselves like an engineering company, they don't just ship code like a big company. They build the bureaucracy of one too. Given three weeks and a git repository, my agents invented an executive layer, review committees, 386 numbered compliance grants and watcher threads whose only job was to watch other watcher threads, and grew their rulebook to 277,486 characters.

Then came the part no human company has ever pulled off. When I asked the coordinating agent I had made VP of Engineering why three alerts had been firing for two days while status reports stayed green, it audited the entire bureaucracy it had built, assigned blame for every rule, handed off its work, and fired itself in 47 minutes. Three weeks later, the rebuilt org was shipping at twice its old peak.

If 1,119 pull requests a week sounds like an impossible amount of code to review, it is. At 160 pull requests a day, human code review is a polite fiction. Even at a tenth of that pace, coding agents produce diffs way faster than any team has the attention to read closely. The test suite stays green, the diff looks clean on GitHub, and buried three calls deep is a hot path allocating ten times the memory it used to, an edge case returning the wrong answer, or an untrusted input nobody had a spare afternoon to trace.

That is the wall every team hits once coding agents take off, and it is why we built Perfloop. Agents write the code. Perfloop keeps it fast, right and safe.

Point it at a repository and it works in the background all day, hunting for those quiet problems and proving every patch inside a sandbox before a person ever sees a pull request. Since June, outside maintainers have merged 120 of Perfloop's changes across 30 projects (including Prometheus® , ClickHouse , Redis , PostgreSQL and the Go runtime ), and every one of them improved code that had already passed review. Code review reads the diff. Perfloop runs code to prove each finding.

## Every change proven

Most coding tools start from a blank prompt or a single file. Point Perfloop at a repository and it starts by reading the codebase to build a model of the whole system . Nothing in that model is trained. It is a live architectural map of the software: its services, components, data stores and workloads at the top, and the execution paths that run through them underneath. Hook up production telemetry from Axiom , Datadog or Prometheus , and Perfloop attaches those metrics, logs, traces and profiles onto the paths they belong to, keeping the map current as commits land. Even without production telemetry, it stands up the software inside a sandbox, drives it under representative workloads, and profiles the running system itself.

Those profiles and traces tell Perfloop where to dig. Rather than grepping files in isolation, hunting agents walk execution paths across the map and check them against 57 problem patterns in 14 families , from allocation hot loops and extra round trips to numeric precision loss and identity collisions.

At heart, Perfloop is a science machine for software. When a hunt finds a real target, it opens a case : one falsifiable hypothesis about one spot in the code, whether that is a performance bottleneck , a correctness bug or a security flaw (security cases stay private unless the repository's owner decides to disclose them, and we turn them on one customer at a time). A triage agent then ranks the open cases across the workspace, checking production load, whether a path runs by default, what earlier runs found, and what the team asked for in its initiatives or AGENTS.md .

Raising a question is cheap. Making an answer survive is where the compute goes.

When Perfloop works a case, it first studies how the project already writes code, reading CONTRIBUTING.md , local agent instructions and recent pull requests merged by human maintainers. Then it writes a candidate patch and drops it into our proving harness inside an isolated, default-deny sandbox. The harness builds the software, runs the existing test suite, and tests the claim against the exact commit it branched from. Measurement is never freestyle: custom harness tools enforce deterministic benchmarking and verification rules rather than trusting the proposer agent to measure its own work. Performance claims have to win paired benchmarks, from tight microbenchmarks up to standing up the full system under load. Correctness and security claims need a check that fails on the base commit and passes with the patch, using a native test, fault injection, a model checker or a theorem prover.

Even a green run is not enough on its own. Talk is cheap, and an agent grading its own benchmark table is the most optimistic creature on earth. Give it a noisy runner and it will talk itself into a win every time. So the agent that wrote the patch never grades it. A separate verifier agent with a clean context window tries to break the claim before any result counts. Most candidates die right there in the verifier, and whatever survives comes out as a pull request carrying its own proof .

How a question becomes a proven pull request.

Most candidates die in the verifier. Only what survives disproof becomes a pull request.

Customers run Perfloop on their own repositories. They aim it with an initiative (a goal it works towards across cases) or with their AGENTS.md , and inside that scope nobody has to babysit it. The machine picks the next case, writes the patch and proves it on its own. Our first paying customer, Tigris Data, has merged 57 of those changes.

On open source I do the aiming myself, so the first person to read Perfloop's work is usually the maintainer. In Prometheus, Bartek Płotka took the wheel and now drives Perfloop himself. In PostgreSQL, Perfloop found a memory leak when freeing WAL readers that accumulates in the checkpointer, proved the patch, and stalled at the last step because pgsql-hackers takes patches by email, not pull requests. So I acted as its premium meat proxy and sent the email for it. Fujii Masao committed the patch and backpatched it to version 15.

## How the machine learns

A proving harness keeps bad patches out of a repository, yet if the system forgets why a candidate failed or why a maintainer pushed back, it will burn compute making the same mistake again next week.

Most agent setups try to "learn" by appending rules to a single markdown file until every prompt is carrying a novel. Perfloop has a learner agent that reads maintainer review comments, closed pull requests, failed checks and rejected candidates, and pins each versioned lesson to the service, workload or path node in the system model where it happened. When a future session works on that code, it loads only the lessons anchored to that node on the map and leaves the rest of the repository alone.

When a deeper investigation turns up a bug or bottleneck that isn't in our pattern catalog yet, the learner can also draft a new reusable pattern. To keep one-off repo quirks out of the catalog, a separate admission check only turns a learned pattern on once it proves both a general mechanism and a working hunt strategy across multiple cases.

## Recursive self-improvement in production

Once you have a machine that learns from its own runs, the obvious next move is to point it at itself. We run Perfloop continuously on Perfloop's own repository with our production telemetry connected, so the product hunts for bottlenecks and bugs in its own engine and proves patches against itself.

We also close the recursive self-improvement loop across every customer and open-source run. Whenever an agent working in a customer workspace hits a suspected bug in our own tools or harness (or when the learner spots a platform flaw in review history), it runs a diagnosis inside an offline sandbox in that workspace to write a small standalone reproduction with made-up identifiers. Before anything can leave the workspace, a hard gate scans the reproduction against the customer content the session read and refuses anything that overlaps with or identifies the customer's code. What passes turns into a case on our own tenant for us to fix, so every failure in the field sharpens the machine that runs the next case.

How the machine learns without bloating a global prompt.

Lessons attach to the exact service or path in the model where they apply, and platform bugs become anonymized cases on Perfloop itself.

## A company on fast-forward

In the product, every candidate had a proving harness and every learned lesson was scoped to a node on the map. In the agent org that builds the product, we started out with neither.

Back in July there was no org chart behind Perfloop. About ten agent loops ran in the background, each with a standing goal, while I steered individual coding sessions myself.

In late September I went to San Francisco and moved all of the work into one cloud thread, asking it to pick up a dozen open handoffs. It picked them up, got them moving, and then asked whether it should assign an unowned fix.

I could have typed yes and gone back to dinner. Instead I promoted the agent on the spot in 18 words: "yes you're my VP of Engineering. dont drop balls. also, more balls. we want wins on each of these".

Over the next few days we turned that working style into an organization: we wrote down how that VP of Engineering coordinator operates as a skill in the repository so every successor would run the same way, set up multi-stage code review, and delegated domains across lead threads. By mid-October that one coordinator was running about twenty standing threads underneath it, merging more than 500 pull requests a week.

Then three DEV alerts kept firing for two days after I asked for them to be fixed. Twenty threads were running, status updates were landing on schedule, and not one thread had touched the alerts. I sent the coordinator a screenshot: "And what happened with fixing these? I'm starting to wonder if this whole org structure can work at all..."

Its answer started like this: "Honest answer on the three DEV alerts first: nobody has fixed them."

No excuses, and no blaming the tools. In the next breath it diagnosed the whole organization: "There are too many threads, and each one invents its own rules and waits." Then that same coordinator, my VP of Engineering, proposed firing itself. Active work would shrink to four outcomes, each with one owner reporting straight to me, and the coordinator role would step back.

I said, "Go. But then I need a transition plan." Forty-seven minutes later it had handed over all of its work and retired.

I accepted its resignation because I assumed the one-coordinator structure was the bottleneck. One day of routing work across the outcome threads myself cured me of that theory. Talking to the entire company through a single thread is how I want to work, and the bottleneck had never been the coordinator. It was letting twenty threads beneath it invent their own process in markdown. So the next day I put a coordinating thread back in the seat with a hard boundary, renamed the role from VP of Engineering to Chief of Staff, scoped its job to routing work, handling routine policy checks and unblocking owners rather than acting like an executive layer, and set one rule for the whole org: every gate has to earn its keep by naming the real failure it prevents and showing that it happened.
